summary: This Informational document gives the problem statement, scenarios, and requirements for Computing-Aware Traffic Steering, which picks servers and directs traffic based on compute capabilities and resources rather than connectivity metrics alone.

plainLanguage.summary: A roadmap and reasons for sending visitors to a restaurant based on how busy the kitchen is, not just distance.

questions: why steer traffic by compute resources
subtitle: Why networks need to steer traffic based on computing resources, not just connectivity.

tldr.problem: Existing traffic routing and load balancing rely on connectivity metrics like distance or latency, but modern distributed services need servers with specific computing capabilities that change dynamically.
tldr.mechanism: Computing-Aware Traffic Steering (CATS) directs traffic to service instances by considering both network metrics and compute resource status (load, CPU, GPU availability), enabling selection of the truly optimal server.
tldr.outcome: Services deployed across edge sites can now match user requests to servers with the right computing resources and network paths, improving latency and reliability for latency-sensitive and compute-heavy applications.

facts.label: Use cases documented
facts.value: 5 (AR/VR, Intelligent Transportation, Digital Twin, SD-WAN, AI)

today: RFC 10054 is Informational and published in October 2026. It is not itself a protocol specification but a problem statement and requirements document that drives the framework defined in RFC 10053. It establishes the need for computing-aware routing in modern edge computing deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.content:
Edge computing deploys services across multiple sites rather than centralizing them in one data center. However, choosing which site should handle each request is difficult. Existing routing uses only connectivity metrics such as hop count, latency, or distance. This leads to suboptimal choices: the closest site might lack sufficient computing resources, or lack the specific resources needed (such as GPUs for AI inference).

Current traffic steering methods include application-layer approaches like ALTO (which requires application modifications) and network-layer approaches like Anycast (which distributes traffic automatically but ignores compute state). Neither accounts for real-time changes in server load, compute capability, or resource availability.

This problem is amplified by client mobility: the optimal server for a client changes as they move, as other clients' demands fluctuate, and as events cause temporary traffic surges.
sections.plainLanguage: When people move around the city or events happen, the busiest restaurant changes. Traffic systems need to know not just where servers are, but whether they have room and the right equipment right now.

sections.title: Use Cases Requiring CATS
sections.content:
Five main use cases illustrate the need for CATS:

AR/VR: Cloud VR requires both low network latency (5.1ms budget for round-trip) and fast rendering (server must complete within 5.5ms). The closest site may have bad network conditions while a farther site has lighter compute load. Optimal selection requires balancing both factors.

Intelligent Transportation: Video processing and AI inference for traffic and driver assistance are compute-heavy and delay-sensitive. When the closest edge site becomes overloaded, CATS can steer delay-insensitive services (in-vehicle entertainment) to distant lighter-loaded sites while keeping latency-critical services local.

Digital Twin: Industrial control systems may virtualize controllers as cloud services. Multiple PLC instances enable load balancing and failover while assets move. High availability and bounded latency are critical; CATS ensures the right instance is selected as physical assets move and load changes.

SD-WAN: Software-defined wide-area networking traditionally uses only network metrics. CATS adds awareness of computing resources at cloud and edge destinations, allowing better selection among application instances deployed in different clouds.

Distributed AI Training and Inference: AI models are split across edge sites. Inference requires balancing token processing capacity (prefilling and decoding stages) with memory for caching. Training requires choosing sites with both network capacity for gradient data and compute resources, optionally favoring green energy sources.
sections.plainLanguage: VR games need to be fast and smooth. Driving warning systems need instant answers. Factories need reliability. Cloud networks need the right computer for the job. AI needs lots of processing power, and sometimes green power. All of these need a smarter way to pick which server to use.

sections.title: Core Requirements
sections.content:
The problem statement drives requirements in five categories:

Instance Selection (R1-R2): The system must dynamically discover which service instances are available, map service IDs to addresses, and assess instance availability based on up-to-date health and load metrics. Metrics must be refreshed at intervals appropriate to the service (millisecond-level for mobile vehicles, second-level for others).

Metric Definition (R3-R10): All implementations must agree on compute-oriented metrics and their representation. An information model (Resource Model) must define how metrics are abstracted from compute and network resources, work across independent implementations, and scale linearly. CATS components must handle metric staleness, use standardized encodings, and avoid routing loops and path oscillations.

Metric Collection and Distribution (R11-R13): The system must collect metrics from service instances, aggregate them hierarchically to reduce overhead, and distribute them to decision makers. It must continue operating even if metric updates are delayed.

Instance Affinity (R14-R16): For stateful services, the system must maintain per-flow affinity to a single instance without requiring applications to manage state transfer. When users or instances move, the system should support continuity (either without re-routing or with explicit state migration).

Confidentiality (R17-R21): User identifying information must be anonymized or hidden using indices. Service instance identities and CS-ID mappings must be authenticated and encrypted. Metric collection must employ integrity checks and encryption, with mechanisms to detect and trace abnormal reports. Cross-node state migration must use end-to-end encryption accessible only to authorized instances.
sections.plainLanguage: The system needs to know what servers are available and how busy they are. Everyone must agree on how to measure "busy." Information must be sent around the network reliably, but without letting everyone see who the users are or giving bad actors a chance to break things.

sections.title: Computing Metrics and Dynamic Selection
sections.content:
Computing metrics differ fundamentally from traditional connectivity metrics. Network metrics like hop count change infrequently, but compute metrics (CPU load, memory usage, job queue depth, GPU availability) change rapidly and in response to user actions.

Different metrics are appropriate for different services. AI inference needs processor cores and memory. VR needs low-latency rendering resources. Transportation scenarios need video decoding capacity. The CATS framework must support heterogeneous metrics that vary by service.

Update frequency presents a trade-off: overly frequent updates create signaling overhead, while infrequent updates lead to stale decisions. The choice depends on service characteristics and network conditions. Fast-moving vehicles may need millisecond-level updates; stationary services may use second-level updates. Metrics must indicate their staleness so that decision-makers know whether to refresh or fall back to less-optimal choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Congestion changes fast, and different services care about different things. A video processor cares about decoding speed; an AI engine cares about processing power. The system must update frequently enough that decisions are fresh, but not so often that messages clog the network.

sections.title: Session Affinity and Stateful Services
sections.content:
When a service is stateful (such as rendering an AR/VR frame, where each frame depends on the previous client input), routing different packets to different instances breaks the service. The system must maintain affinity on a per-flow basis, ensuring all packets of a flow reach the same instance.

However, creating fine-grained per-flow state in network devices is expensive. Instead, CATS should rely on higher-layer (application) logic to indicate affinity requirements and, when needed, migrate state to a new instance if the best instance changes (for example, due to client mobility or metric changes).

Stateless services (where each request is independent) do not require affinity beyond a single request. In these cases, CATS can load-balance at packet or request granularity. The challenge is supporting both stateless and stateful services without burdening network infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: If a program is remembering something between messages (like a video game remembering the previous frame), you cannot suddenly switch servers mid-game. But if each message is independent, you can split them around to balance the load.

left.title: Network only
left.desc: Pick the site with the shortest network path.

right.title: Network + Compute
right.desc: Pick the site with the best network path AND available compute.
